One is that you make a list of the stocks you want to buy, and you buy them. If you have a good reason to buy a stock, you buy it; if not, not. The default is not. If you have no opinions about a stock, you don’t buy it. The other is that you make a list of the stocks in the world, and for each stock on the list, you ask yourself: “Do I have a reason to overweight or underweight this stock?” The default is owning the market portfolio: If you have no opinions about a stock, or ambivalent or confused opinions, you tend to just own the average amount of the stock, its market capitalization weighting in the market portfolio. If you have reason to think that the stock is better than the market thinks it is, buy more of it. If you have reason to think that it’s worse than the market thinks it is, buy less of it, or zero, or go short. But you start from the premise that the market has a pretty good idea of what stocks to own, and that if you have no special information, then you should just do what the market tells you. I think it is fair to say that the second approach — defaulting to the market weight and overweighting or underweighting when you have reason to — was virtually unheard-of 100 years ago and is quite standard now. Many, many investors mostly buy index funds: They assume that the market knows better than they do, so they buy the stocks that the market likes. But many active investors use the same intellectual framework: They run large diversified portfolios and pick stocks to overweight and underweight against the background assumption that the default is the market weight. [1] The two approaches suggest different ideas of risk. In the first approach, each stock is risky, and you should only make a risky bet on a stock if you have a good reason to. In the second approach, investors expect to earn the market return on average, and there is symmetrical risk around that return. If the market returns 8% and you earn 2%, that’s bad; in the relevant sense you have lost 6%. A company says it wants to raise $1 billion by selling 100 million shares at $10 each. Its bankers go out to investors, who put in orders for the shares. The bankers collect orders for, say, 700 million shares. “The IPO is seven times oversubscribed,” they say. [1] The IPO prices, and the bankers and company get together to “allocate” the IPO: There are orders for 700 million shares, but the company is selling only 100 million shares (actually 115 million with the greenshoe ), so most of the orders won’t get filled. The banks and company will favor some investors (long-term investors who understand the company’s story, the banks’ favorite clients, retail, whatever) and zero others (fast-money hedge funds that will flip the shares, etc.), but even the favored investors will probably get cut back. If you put in an order for 10 million shares, and the book is seven times covered, you’re not realistically going to get more than 5 million, and 2 million is more likely. But you know that, of course. If you have a sense that it will be a hot IPO — for instance because your salesperson at the bank says “this is a hot IPO and we’re getting a lot of demand” — you can scale up your order to try to get more shares. If you want 5 million shares, put in an order for 20 million. That way you’ll probably get cut back to 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 million. Sometimes you’ll mis-calibrate and end up with 1 million, or 10 million, either of which would be bad. (If you get 1 million, you’ll have to buy more when the stock starts trading, and if you got cut back to 1 million that probably means it will trade up. If you get 10 million, the reverse: You’ll have to sell when the stock starts trading, and if you got allocated so many shares, that’s a bad sign for demand.) But in a hot IPO, many investors are putting in orders for more shares than they want. [2] Or that is the stereotype. I have sometimes wondered if it applies to the new wave of mega-IPOs. If you are an environmental investor, sometimes you put environmental concerns above shareholder returns. If you are a social investor, sometimes you put social concerns above shareholder returns. Governance is different: Governance means making sure that the managers of a company put shareholder returns above their own interests. If environmental, social and governance investing has good performance — if ESG stocks go up — it stands to reason that a lot of that performance would come from the governance. I don’t really want to argue for this analysis, which is debatable in various ways, [1] but there is something to it. “Governance” is, traditionally, about shareholder value, about how the profits of a company are split between its managers and its owners. Finance and legal academics noticed that, if a company makes a lot of money, the bandits in charge of the company could keep all the money for themselves and not give any of it to shareholders. “The premise behind modern corporate finance in general,” writes Jean Tirole on the first page of Chapter 1 of his corporate finance textbook , “is that corporate insiders need not act in the best interests of the providers of the funds.” Governance is about keeping an eye on the managers, so they do not become bandits, so the shareholders can get some of the money. This works very well in textbooks, but in the real world you have to take account of the particular skills and characteristics of particular bandits. Every so often, Elon Musk will go to the board of directors of Tesla Inc. and hint “hey, nice company you have here, it would be a shame if I were to go build robots elsewhere and break some stuff on my way out,” and the board will give him an extra trillion dollars. Banditry! But the shareholders do not complain, much, because Musk’s idiosyncratic personal involvement really is crucial to Tesla being worth a trillion dollars in the first place. Happy Anthropic IPO day You know the basic theory of AI circular financing , right? It’s: If you give Anthropic PBC a certain amount of money — say $74 — you get a share of Anthropic stock. This gives you partial ownership of Anthropic’s future profits. If those profits are high, the stock will go up and you will make money. If Google gives Anthropic the same amount of money ($74), it gets a share of Anthropic stock, and if the stock goes up Google will make money. But Google also gets something else. Anthropic has agreed to pay Google something like $250 billion for computing capacity over the next seven years. [1] Anthropic does not currently have $250 billion, although it is increasingly cash-flow positive, and it is not exactly an investment-grade credit . The more money Anthropic has, the better its chances of actually paying Google that $250 billion. In some loose sense, the money that Google gives Anthropic for stock comes back to Google as revenue. Plus it gets the stock. For “Google” you could substitute “Nvidia” or “Broadcom” or “AMD” or “TSMC” or a number of other giant providers of picks and shovels to the artificial intelligence industry. One conclusion you could take away from this is, like, ooh the AI industry is a house of cards, ooh the revenue is all fake, ooh, ooh. That’s definitely a conclusion that people draw, but it doesn’t seem especially compelled by this description, and I am not going to spend any time on it. Another conclusion you could take away, though, is just that Anthropic stock is worth more to Google than it is to you. Every dollar that Google invests in Anthropic gets it (1) some Anthropic stock and (2) some revenue; every dollar that you invest in Anthropic gets you just the Anthropic stock. Google’s package is more valuable than your package. I almost added “… so Google should pay more for it,” but that doesn’t strictly follow.
